segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Be careful not to practice your righteousness in front of people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet ahead of you, as the performers do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be praised by people. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that your giving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when you pray, you must not be like the performers, for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the main streets, so that they may be seen by people. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when you pray, do not babble on like the Gentiles, for they think that they will be heard because of their many words.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Pray, then, in this way: ‘Our Father in the heavens, may your name be held holy,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: may your kingdom come, may your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Give us today our daily bread.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And do not bring us into testing, but rescue us from the evil one.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For if you forgive people their offenses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your offenses.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the performers, for they make their faces unsightly so that they may be seen by people to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that you may be seen to be fasting not by people but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in or steal.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The lamp of the body is the eye. So if your eye is generous, your whole body will be full of light;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but if your eye is stingy, your whole body will be full of darkness. So if the light in you is darkness, how great that darkness is!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one can be a slave to two masters, for he will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot be slaves to God and to wealth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this reason I tell you: do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look at the birds of the sky: they do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they are?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And which of you by worrying can add a single hour to your span of life?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And why do you worry about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labor or spin.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if this is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, you of little faith?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.

notes.note: Here the word means the practice of religious duty; the three examples that follow are giving to the needy, prayer and fasting. Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), and some scholars prefer “justice”. Some later manuscripts read “almsgiving” in this verse, which is why the King James Version has “alms”.

The Greek is plural here and in verse 9, a Semitic turn of phrase that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”. Where the Greek is singular (verses 10 and 20) the text has “heaven”, and it has “sky” where the visible sky is meant (verse 26).

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a stage actor, and in this passage the picture of a performance is active: a trumpet, street corners, an audience. Jewish Greek before the New Testament already used the word for a godless or insincere person, which is why most translations have “hypocrites” here. “Performers” is used in verses 2, 5 and 16 because the charge in each case is doing religion in order to be seen.

notes.phrase: they have been paid their reward in full
notes.note: The verb is the standard term on surviving receipts of the period for payment received in full, so hearers would have caught a commercial tone: the account is settled and nothing more is owed. Older translations have “they have their reward”; many modern ones have “they have received their reward in full”.

notes.traditional: use vain repetitions; heap up empty phrases
notes.note: The Greek verb is very rare and its exact sense is uncertain; it may imitate the sound of stammering or meaningless chatter. The next clause, about “many words”, shows that the fault is wordiness meant to win a hearing. Other translations have “use vain repetitions” or “heap up empty phrases”.

notes.phrase: may your name be held holy
notes.note: The verb is built on the ordinary Greek word for “holy”. With God’s name as its object it means to treat or acknowledge as holy, not to make holy. “Hallowed” says the same thing but is no longer current English; the meaning is not in dispute. Many scholars take the passive as a request that God himself bring this about.

The Greek word is almost unknown outside the Lord’s Prayer and its meaning is uncertain. The main proposals are “for the coming day”, “necessary for existence” and “for today”. With no secure alternative, the traditional “daily” is kept.

In the usage of the period, including the Greek Old Testament, the word chiefly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will stay faithful. English “temptation” has narrowed to enticement to sin and could suggest that God lures people into wrongdoing. Most versions keep “temptation” and some have “time of trial”; scholars disagree about which sense is in view here, so this rendering is an editorial choice.

The Greek form can be masculine (“the evil one”, meaning the devil) or neuter (“evil”). The traditional wording of the prayer has “evil”. Many modern translations and scholars prefer “the evil one”, since Matthew uses the same expression for the devil elsewhere (13:19, 13:38), but the question remains open.

notes.phrase: rescue us from the evil one
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add a closing doxology: “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.” It is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is generally regarded as a later addition from the prayer’s use in worship, so it is not part of the Greek text translated here.

The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. The traditional “trespasses” now chiefly suggests entering property without permission. It is a different word from “debts” in verse 12, which reflects a Jewish way of speaking of sins as debts owed to God.

The Greek word literally means “eating”. It may refer to the corrosion of metal, which is the traditional understanding, or to insects or vermin that eat stored goods, as some modern translations take it.

The Greek word means single or sincere, and related words are used of open-handed giving. The saying stands between treasure in heaven and slavery to wealth, and it is paired with the “evil eye”, a known idiom for stinginess, so “generous” fits the context. Most translations have “healthy” or “sound”, keeping the physical picture of an eye that lets in light, and mention generosity in a footnote; that picture is less visible in this rendering.

The Greek says “evil”. An “evil eye” is a Jewish idiom for a grudging, tight-fisted attitude (for example Deuteronomy 15:9; compare Matthew 20:15). Most translations have “evil”, “bad” or “unhealthy”, which keeps the physical image; the rendering here follows from “generous” in verse 22.

The verb means to serve as a slave, someone wholly owned by a master. Most translations have “serve”, which is accurate but lets a modern reader picture a job that could be split between two employers.

The Greek keeps an Aramaic word for wealth or property, traditionally carried into English as “Mammon”; modern translations have “money” or “wealth”. The saying pictures it as a rival master, but there is no evidence that it was the name of a deity.

notes.phrase: a single hour to your span of life
notes.note: The Greek says “add one cubit”, a length of about eighteen inches, to a word that can mean either age or height. The King James Version has “one cubit unto his stature”. Most modern translations take the cubit as a figure for a short stretch of time added to a lifespan, since the saying calls for a small addition, not a large one.

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural it commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples, and it is translated “Gentiles” or “nations” according to context. In verse 7 “Gentiles” translates a closely related adjective.

Many manuscripts read “the kingdom of God and his righteousness”. The Greek text translated here has only “the kingdom and his righteousness”, where “his” refers to the Father of verse 32 and is taken to apply to both nouns.

candidates.reason: An Aramaic word left untranslated in the Greek, occurring only four times (here and Luke 16); versions vary between “Mammon”, “money” and “wealth”, and it may qualify for loanword treatment.
Recurs across the Gospels and Paul, and the choice between “serve” and “be a slave to” should match whatever is decided for δοῦλος.
Recurs in Matthew, Luke, 1 Corinthians and Philippians, where versions waver between “worry”, “be anxious” and “care for”.
Recurs in Matthew, Luke and Acts; “alms” is archaic, and the alternatives (“charity”, “gifts to the poor”, “giving to the needy”) should not vary from book to book.
The substantive with the article recurs (Matthew 5:37, 5:39, 13:19; John 17:15; Ephesians 6:16; 1 John), and the choice between “evil” and “the evil one” needs a consistent policy.
